title: Amateur Radio in New Zealand: Beginner Guide | ZL3TOM
description: How to get started with amateur radio in New Zealand, including the GAOC, callsigns, the shared GURL, NZART resources and your first station.
content: ZL3TOM beginner guide Amateur Radio in New Zealand: Beginner Guide How to get started with amateur radio in New Zealand, including the GAOC, callsigns, the shared GURL, NZART resources and your first station. ← All guides 01 How amateur licensing works in New Zealand New Zealand amateur operators share a General User Radio Licence (GURL) . You do not apply for a separate station licence or pay an individual radio-licence fee, but you must hold a current General Amateur Operator's Certificate (GAOC) and callsign before transmitting. The GURL sets the legal conditions for ordinary amateur operation. It does not authorise every activity: beacons, repeaters and fixed links have separate licensing arrangements. 02 Get your certificate and callsign Learn the radio theory, regulations and safe operating practices covered by the amateur examination. Contact an Approved Radio Examiner listed by RSM ↗ . Sit the examination and follow the examiner's current process for obtaining a callsign. Check that your certificate and callsign are recorded in the Register of Radio Frequencies. An examiner may charge for the examination or callsign process even though the shared GURL itself has no individual licence fee. 03 Choose a sensible first station A VHF/UHF handheld is an accessible way to learn local simplex and repeater operation. Before buying, check which repeaters and activity are actually available around your QTH. An external antenna often improves a handheld more than extra transmitter power. HF opens longer-distance contacts but needs more space, antenna planning and attention to propagation. Start with equipment you can operate safely and learn well. 04 Know the difference between rules and band plans The RSM GURL provides the legal authority and conditions. The NZART band plan coordinates how amateurs use the available spectrum so different activities can coexist. Check both before transmitting. Always check the live documents: allocations, conditions and coordinated calling or repeater channels can change. A saved screenshot may be out of date. 05 Make your first call Program the correct frequency, mode, repeater offset and access tone where required. Listen long enough to be sure the channel is free. Give your callsign clearly and say that you are listening. Keep the first transmission short and leave a pause between overs. Write down the other station's callsign and contact details. SIMPLE FIRST CALL ZL3TOM listening. 06 Build good habits from day one Use the minimum power needed for a reliable contact. Identify with your callsign and keep transmissions courteous. Learn RF exposure, electrical and antenna safety before installing equipment. Join a local club or listen to experienced operators. Keep the current RSM licence conditions and NZART band plan bookmarked. Official sources Software and network details change. Check these official pages before installing or entering account information. title: New Zealand Amateur Radio Band Plans: Beginner Guide | ZL3TOM
description: A beginner guide to New Zealand amateur radio band plans, legal licence conditions, common HF and VHF/UHF bands, modes and checks before transmitting.
content: ZL3TOM beginner guide New Zealand Amateur Radio Band Plans: Beginner Guide A beginner guide to New Zealand amateur radio band plans, legal licence conditions, common HF and VHF/UHF bands, modes and checks before transmitting. ← All guides 01 Licence conditions and band plans are different The RSM Amateur Radio Operators GURL is the legal authority for eligible New Zealand amateurs to transmit. The NZART band plan is the operating coordination guide used to reduce interference between modes and activities. A band-plan segment is not permission by itself. Your certificate, the current GURL, equipment and any location-specific restriction still control what you may legally do. 02 A quick orientation to common bands Band Common beginner uses 80 m and 40 m Regional and longer-range HF voice, CW and digital contacts. 30 m, 20 m and 17 m HF CW, data and international contacts; mode permissions differ by band. 15 m, 12 m and 10 m Long-distance contacts when propagation supports them. 6 m VHF weak-signal, local and occasional long-distance activity. 2 m and 70 cm Local simplex, repeaters, satellites and digital voice. 23 cm and above Repeaters, data, satellites and microwave experimentation. This table is only an orientation. Use the current NZART plan for actual frequencies, bandwidths, calling channels and repeater allocations. 03 Read the plan before choosing a frequency Find the correct band and mode section. Check the authorised frequency range in the current GURL. Check the NZART plan for calling frequencies and coordinated mode segments. Allow for the full occupied bandwidth of your signal, especially near a band edge. Listen for existing activity and identify any local repeater input or output. 04 HF, VHF and UHF need different habits On HF, propagation, signal bandwidth and international band planning matter. On VHF/UHF, correct repeater offsets, access tones, simplex channels and local coordination are common concerns. Satellite operation needs Doppler adjustment and careful power use. The NZART band-usage guide complements the printable plan and explains recommended operating practices for New Zealand. 05 Be especially careful with special allocations Do not assume that a band available in another country has identical New Zealand conditions. Some allocations can have special power, mode, location or interference-protection requirements. The 60-metre area is one example where you should read the current GURL and NZART guidance before transmitting. 06 Five checks before you press PTT Am I authorised for this frequency and operation? Is my whole signal inside the permitted band? Am I following the current coordinated band plan? Is the frequency already in use? Are my power, antenna and station settings safe and appropriate? title: USA Amateur Radio Band Plans: Beginner Guide | ZL3TOM
description: A clear guide to USA amateur radio bands, FCC licence classes, ARRL band plans and the checks operators should make before transmitting.
content: ZL3TOM beginner guide USA Amateur Radio Band Plans: Beginner Guide A clear guide to USA amateur radio bands, FCC licence classes, ARRL band plans and the checks operators should make before transmitting. ← All guides 01 Why a New Zealand operator may need the US plan Knowing the US allocations helps when working American stations on HF, visiting the United States or following a US-based net or event. US privileges are not the same as New Zealand privileges, and US operators must stay within the sub-bands allowed by their licence class. 02 The three US licence classes Technician Entry-level privileges with broad VHF/UHF access and limited privileges on some HF bands. General Much wider HF privileges as well as VHF/UHF access. Amateur Extra The widest amateur privileges, including additional HF sub-band access. Always use the current FCC and ARRL information because exact frequency and mode privileges matter. 03 Common US amateur bands at a glance Range group Common bands Typical activity HF 160, 80, 40, 30, 20, 17, 15, 12 and 10 m Voice, CW, data and long-distance contacts, subject to class and mode limits. Low VHF 6 m Local, weak-signal and propagation openings. VHF 2 m and 1.25 m Simplex, repeaters, satellites and weak-signal work. UHF 70 cm and higher Repeaters, satellites, data, digital voice and experimentation. This is not a frequency-authorisation table. Consult the current ARRL chart and FCC Part 97 for the precise limits that apply. 04 Allocations and voluntary band plans FCC Part 97 contains the binding rules. ARRL band plans are voluntary operating arrangements that divide bands into commonly used mode and activity segments. Following them reduces avoidable interference, but they do not expand your legal privileges. 05 Avoid band-edge mistakes Check the operator's licence class and the exact authorised sub-band. Allow for the entire occupied signal, not just the displayed dial frequency. Check mode and emission restrictions. Use no more transmitter power than needed for reliable communication. Listen before calling and respect established activity. 06 Working US stations from New Zealand You operate under New Zealand rules at your transmitter; the US station operates under FCC rules at theirs. Agree on a frequency that is legal for both operators, use UTC when arranging or logging the QSO, and move if either station is too close to a band edge. Official sources Software and network details change. Check these official pages before installing or entering account information. title: Amateur Radio Operating Basics Guide | ZL3TOM
description: A practical guide to operating confidently across HF, VHF, UHF, repeaters, digital modes, and linked systems.
content: ZL3TOM guide Amateur Radio Operating Basics A practical guide to operating confidently across HF, VHF, UHF, repeaters, digital modes, and linked systems. All guides 01 Before you transmit Listen first and confirm the frequency or repeater is clear. Set audio and power levels cleanly for the mode you are using. Know whether the frequency is a calling channel, repeater, net, or digital segment. Have your log ready with UTC time, band, mode, and callsign. 02 HF operation and calling CQ CQ is mainly used on HF and some digital modes. Keep calls clear and unhurried. ON-AIR EXAMPLE CQ CQ CQ, this is ZL3TOM, ZL3TOM calling CQ and standing by. 03 VHF and UHF simplex On VHF and UHF, calls are often made on a calling channel, then moved off. ON-AIR EXAMPLE ZL3TOM listening. 04 Repeaters and linked systems Pause briefly after keying up so links activate. Identify clearly and invite replies. Keep transmissions concise, especially on wide-area systems. 05 Digital modes Clean audio matters more than power. Follow band plans and recommended frequencies. Monitor your signal and stop if you cause interference. 06 Logging and good practice Log contacts accurately using UTC. Identify regularly and at the end of your over. Leave pauses so others can join or break in. Be welcoming, patient, and respectful. Written by Thomas Bernard — ZL3TOM Last updated: 3 September 2026 Good operating Listen first. Identify clearly. Leave a pause. Be patient and welcoming. Suggest a guide

title: HF CQ and Contacts Guide | ZL3TOM
description: Practical tips for HF calling, answering, handling busy conditions, and finishing a QSO cleanly.
content: ZL3TOM guide HF CQ and Contacts Practical tips for HF calling, answering, handling busy conditions, and finishing a QSO cleanly. All guides 01 1. Find a clear frequency Listen for at least 10 to 20 seconds — longer if conditions are busy or weak. Check whether the frequency is used for a net, DX activity, or a common calling spot. If you are unsure, ask once, then listen again. ON-AIR EXAMPLE Is this frequency in use, is this frequency in use, ZL3TOM. 02 2. Calling CQ on SSB Short beats fancy. Repeat your callsign clearly, then listen rather than calling constantly. ON-AIR EXAMPLE CQ CQ CQ, this is ZL3TOM, ZL3TOM calling CQ and standing by. 03 3. Answering a CQ Say their callsign once, then your callsign once. Slow is smooth; smooth is fast. ON-AIR EXAMPLE ZL3ABC, this is ZL3TOM. 04 4. Your first over Make the contact easy to log: confirm callsigns, then give a report, your name, and your location. ON-AIR EXAMPLE ZL3ABC, thanks for the call. You are 5 and 9 in Christchurch. Name Thomas, over. 05 5. Signal reports Give a report that feels fair. For a weak signal, explain kindly: ‘You are 4 and 7, readable with a bit of noise.’ Ask for repeats when needed — never guess a callsign. 06 6. Handling pileups Take one station at a time and confirm the callsign before logging. Keep overs short so the frequency keeps flowing. If you cannot copy, ask for the callsign again. ON-AIR EXAMPLE Only the station ending in ABC, again please. 07 7. End cleanly Thank the operator, confirm final callsigns, and say whether you are staying on frequency. ON-AIR EXAMPLE Thanks for the contact, 73. This is ZL3TOM clear and listening. Written by Thomas Bernard — ZL3TOM Last updated: 3 September 2026 Good operating Listen first. Identify clearly. Leave a pause. Be patient and welcoming. Suggest a guide

title: Repeaters and Nets Guide | ZL3TOM
description: Use amateur radio repeaters and participate in nets confidently, including AllStar and EchoLink linked systems.
content: ZL3TOM guide Repeaters and Nets Use amateur radio repeaters and participate in nets confidently, including AllStar and EchoLink linked systems. All guides 01 Repeater basics Listen first to make sure the repeater is clear. Key the microphone, pause for a second, then speak. Identify clearly and leave pauses between overs. Keep transmissions within the repeater timeout. 02 Monitoring and calling If nobody replies, wait and try once more. If the repeater is busy, keep transmissions short. ON-AIR EXAMPLE ZL3ABC, ZL3ABC, this is ZL3TOM. 03 Joining a conversation Wait for a clear gap, then say your callsign once. If invited in, keep your first over short. If it is a directed net or important traffic, stand by. 04 Linked systems Allow extra pauses for network delay. Keep topics appropriate for a wide audience. Avoid kerchunking; identify briefly if you key accidentally. Remember that many operators share the link. 05 Checking into a net Wait for net control to request check-ins. Give your callsign, location, and whether you have traffic. ON-AIR EXAMPLE Net control, ZL3TOM, Christchurch, no traffic. 06 Passing messages Write everything down before transmitting. Read back important details to confirm accuracy. Use phonetics for names, places, and numbers if copy is weak. Written by Thomas Bernard — ZL3TOM Last updated: 3 September 2026 Good operating Listen first. Identify clearly. Leave a pause. Be patient and welcoming. Suggest a guide

title: Audio and Levels Guide | ZL3TOM
description: Quick, practical settings and habits for clean audio on SSB, FM, CW, and digital modes.
content: ZL3TOM guide Audio and Levels Quick, practical settings and habits for clean audio on SSB, FM, CW, and digital modes. All guides 01 The goal: sound clean On every mode, the easiest station to work is the station that sounds clean and steady. Loud does not equal good — clean equals good. 02 SSB mic gain and processing Set mic gain so your voice is strong but not distorted. Use compression or speech processing lightly. Keep a consistent mic distance and speak across the mic to reduce pops. ON-AIR EXAMPLE If people say you are splattering or your audio is crunchy, reduce gain or processing. 03 FM and handheld habits Use a normal voice and normal mic distance. Talking too close often causes muffled audio or clipping. On repeaters, key up, pause, then talk. 04 Digital drive level Start with low audio drive and increase slowly. Aim for minimal or no ALC movement on many radios. Turn off speech processing for sound-card digital modes. ON-AIR EXAMPLE Clean digital beats extra power, every time. 05 Quick checklist ON-AIR EXAMPLE SSB: no distortion, light processing FM: normal deviation, do not shout Digital: low drive, minimal ALC All: steady pace, clear callsign Written by Thomas Bernard — ZL3TOM Last updated: 3 September 2026 Good operating Listen first. Identify clearly. Leave a pause. Be patient and welcoming. Suggest a guide

title: Antenna Basics Guide | ZL3TOM
description: Simple antenna fundamentals that help you get better results without overcomplicating your station.
content: ZL3TOM guide Antenna Basics Simple antenna fundamentals that help you get better results without overcomplicating your station. All guides 01 The antenna matters most A better antenna system usually improves results more than upgrading radios. Start simple, get on air, then improve one thing at a time. 02 Three basics that always help Height helps, especially for VHF and UHF. Clear space helps — stay away from metal roofs, gutters, and power lines. Good feedline helps, especially on VHF and above where coax loss can be high. 03 Coax and connectors Choose coax that suits the run length and band. Weatherproof every outdoor join. Use strain relief so connectors do not carry weight. 04 Understanding SWR Low SWR can protect your radio and keep power transfer efficient. Perfect SWR does not guarantee performance; pattern and height matter too. If SWR is high, stop and check connectors, coax, and antenna length. ON-AIR EXAMPLE Fix safety and reliability first, tune for SWR second, then chase performance. 05 Safety comes first Keep antennas well clear of power lines — always. Secure masts and guy lines for serious wind loads. Plan grounding and lightning protection for your situation. Written by Thomas Bernard — ZL3TOM Last updated: 3 September 2026 Good operating Listen first. Identify clearly. Leave a pause. Be patient and welcoming. Suggest a guide

title: Q Codes and Jargon Guide | ZL3TOM
description: Common Q codes, when they help, and when plain language is the better choice.
content: ZL3TOM guide Q Codes and Jargon Common Q codes, when they help, and when plain language is the better choice. All guides 01 Why Q codes exist Q codes are short signals that save time, especially on CW. They are also used on voice and digital, but you only need a handful for most contacts. 02 The most useful Q codes ON-AIR EXAMPLE QTH location QRM interference from other stations QRN noise QSB fading QSY change frequency QRZ who is calling me? QSL confirmation QRP low power QRO high power QRT stop transmitting 03 How they sound on voice ‘QTH Christchurch’ means ‘my location is Christchurch.’ ‘Lots of QRM’ means ‘I have interference from other stations.’ ‘Let’s QSY’ means ‘let’s change frequency.’ 04 When plain language is better Plain language sounds natural on repeaters and local chats. Explain terms to new operators rather than stacking jargon. Simple words can be clearer when copy is weak. 05 Two rules that prevent mistakes If you did not copy a callsign, ask again — do not guess. If you are unsure what someone means, ask. Most operators are happy to explain. Written by Thomas Bernard — ZL3TOM Last updated: 3 September 2026 Good operating Listen first. Identify clearly. Leave a pause. Be patient and welcoming. Suggest a guide

title: Emergency Comms Basics Guide | ZL3TOM
description: Clear, calm habits for message passing, priority traffic, and directed nets.
content: ZL3TOM guide Emergency Comms Basics Clear, calm habits for message passing, priority traffic, and directed nets. All guides 01 The goal: clear communication In emergency-style traffic, clarity and calm matter more than radio jargon. Keep messages short, accurate, and confirmed. 02 Directed nets The net control station manages the flow; wait to be called in. Use short transmissions, identify clearly, then stand by. If you double with someone, stop and try again when invited. ON-AIR EXAMPLE Net control, ZL3TOM, Christchurch, no traffic. 03 Message handling Record who it is to, who it is from, and the message content. Repeat names, addresses, phone numbers, and counts. Read back key parts and confirm what you copied. ON-AIR EXAMPLE To: [name or agency] From: [name or station] Message: [short, clear content] Time: [UTC] Date: [UTC] 04 Priority and emergency breaks Use priority or emergency breaks only when genuinely needed. Keep the wording short so net control can respond quickly. ON-AIR EXAMPLE Break, priority traffic Break, emergency traffic 05 Voice discipline Use phonetics for names and locations when copy is weak. Pause between overs, especially on linked systems. If you are relaying, clearly say so and identify who you are relaying for. Never guess callsigns, names, or numbers. Written by Thomas Bernard — ZL3TOM Last updated: 3 September 2026 Good operating Listen first. Identify clearly. Leave a pause. Be patient and welcoming. Suggest a guide

title: How to Install and Use EchoLink | ZL3TOM
description: A beginner-friendly EchoLink setup guide for Windows, Android, iPhone and the web, including callsign validation, audio checks and your first contact.
content: ZL3TOM beginner guide How to Install and Use EchoLink A beginner-friendly EchoLink setup guide for Windows, Android, iPhone and the web, including callsign validation, audio checks and your first contact. ← All guides 01 What EchoLink does EchoLink lets licensed amateur radio operators connect through internet-linked stations. You can use an app directly, or connect through a local repeater or link that is already on EchoLink. Callsigns ending in -L are link stations and -R identifies repeater stations. A plain callsign is normally an individual user. 02 Choose the official version EchoLink is available from the official site for Windows, Android and iOS, with EchoLink Web available in a browser. Download from the official source rather than an unofficial app store listing or download mirror. Start here: Official EchoLink downloads and web access ↗ 03 Register and validate your callsign Install and open EchoLink, then enter your amateur radio callsign. Choose a strong password that you do not reuse elsewhere. Complete the official validation process and provide the requested proof of licence. Wait until your callsign is approved before trying to connect. EchoLink access is for licensed amateur radio operators. Use your own callsign and keep your licence details current. 04 Set up clear audio Allow microphone access when your phone or computer asks. Select the correct microphone and speaker or headset. Keep the microphone level moderate; loud or distorted audio is harder to understand. Use headphones if speaker audio is feeding back into the microphone. Listen to a conversation before transmitting. On a linked network, leave a short pause after the other station unkeys so links can reset and another operator can join. 05 Make your first connection Search by callsign, location or node number. Select a station and connect. Listen first and check the channel is free. Press transmit, pause briefly, then give your callsign and say you are listening. Release transmit fully when you finish each over. Disconnect when your contact is complete. ON-AIR EXAMPLE ZL3TOM listening through EchoLink. 06 Common EchoLink problems Callsign not accepted Complete validation and make sure the callsign matches your licence. No audio Check microphone permission, input/output device selection and system volume. Cannot connect Try another station and the app's relay or proxy option. Some routers and networks restrict direct connections. Echo or feedback Use headphones and lower speaker or microphone volume. Official sources Software and network details change. Check these official pages before installing or entering account information. title: How to Get a DMR ID for Amateur Radio | ZL3TOM
description: Learn what a DMR ID is, how licensed amateur radio operators register through RadioID, and where to enter the ID in a radio, hotspot and BrandMeister account.
content: ZL3TOM beginner guide How to Get a DMR ID for Amateur Radio Learn what a DMR ID is, how licensed amateur radio operators register through RadioID, and where to enter the ID in a radio, hotspot and BrandMeister account. ← All guides 01 What a DMR ID is A DMR ID is a numeric identity associated with a licensed amateur radio operator. Digital Mobile Radio networks use it to identify your transmissions and display your callsign information. Your callsign remains your legal on-air identification. The number does not replace good operating practice or the requirements of your local licence. 02 Register through RadioID Go to the official RadioID website ↗ . Create an account using your real details and licensed callsign. Follow the current application process and upload the licence evidence requested for your country. Check every entry before submitting; your callsign and identity need to match the evidence. Wait for approval, then record your assigned ID somewhere safe. The website and verification steps can change. Follow the instructions shown by RadioID rather than an old screenshot or unofficial video. 03 Put the ID in the right places DMR radio: enter the ID in your radio's codeplug or programming software. Hotspot: set the same operator ID in the hotspot dashboard. Do not copy another operator's number. Network account: if you use BrandMeister, create or update your self-care profile with the same callsign and ID. Software app: enter your ID only where the official app documentation requests it. Back up your codeplug before editing it, and confirm the radio shows your own ID before transmitting. 04 DMR terms you will meet Talkgroup A numbered conversation group, such as worldwide BrandMeister talkgroup 91. Time slot On many DMR repeaters, two independent voice paths share one radio channel. Use the slot specified by the repeater or talkgroup plan. Colour code A DMR access setting, similar in purpose to a repeater access tone. It must match the repeater. Codeplug The saved radio configuration containing channels, contacts, zones and your DMR ID. 05 Protect your accounts Use a unique password for RadioID and each network account. Never publish hotspot security passwords or IAX credentials. Use the official password-reset process if access is lost. Update your record if your callsign changes. 06 Your first DMR contact Load a known local repeater or hotspot channel, select the correct talkgroup, and listen before transmitting. Key up, pause briefly, give your callsign, and say you are listening. Leave extra space between overs because linked networks need time to switch. ON-AIR EXAMPLE ZL3TOM listening on talkgroup 91. title: Useful Amateur Radio Apps for Phone and Computer | ZL3TOM
description: A practical guide to useful amateur radio apps for logging, programming, APRS, weak-signal modes, EchoLink and linked digital voice on phones and computers.
content: ZL3TOM beginner guide Useful Amateur Radio Apps for Phone and Computer A practical guide to useful amateur radio apps for logging, programming, APRS, weak-signal modes, EchoLink and linked digital voice on phones and computers. ← All guides 01 Choose an app for a job The best radio app is the one that solves a clear problem. Start with one logger and the official programming software for your radio, then add tools as your operating interests grow. Platform support changes, so check each official download page before installing. Never enter radio-network credentials into an unknown app or website. 02 Programming: CHIRP CHIRP ↗ is a free, open-source tool that can program many amateur radios. It is useful for organising repeaters, simplex channels and memory names. Confirm that your exact radio model is supported. Use the correct data cable and driver. Download from the radio before editing. Save an untouched backup before uploading changes. 03 Weak-signal digital modes: WSJT-X WSJT-X ↗ is desktop software for weak-signal amateur radio communication. It is widely used for modes including FT8 and FT4. Accurate computer time, correct radio control, and clean audio levels matter. Check your licence conditions, band plan and frequency before transmitting. 04 APRS: APRSdroid and APRS.fi APRSdroid ↗ provides APRS features on Android, including position, nearby stations and messages. APRS.fi ↗ is a convenient browser map for looking up stations such as ZL3TOM ↗ . Think carefully before beaconing a home or private location. Only transmit on amateur frequencies if you are licensed and your setup follows local rules. 05 Portable logging: Ham2K PoLo Ham2K Portable Logger ↗ is designed for portable logging on Android and iOS. It can help organise activations and export contacts for your main log. After an activation, review callsigns, UTC times, bands and modes before uploading contacts to an online logbook. 06 Linked voice: EchoLink and QSO One EchoLink ↗ connects licensed operators and internet-linked stations. QSO One ↗ combines several linked voice systems in one app, including AllStarLink, EchoLink, DMR, System Fusion and M17. Complete any required callsign or network validation first. Treat node and hotspot credentials like passwords. 07 Logging and backups A browser-based logbook such as a self-hosted Cloudlog site can keep contacts in one place. Whatever logger you choose, export regular ADIF backups and store a copy somewhere separate from the device. Use UTC for contact times. Record the correct callsign, band and mode. Add useful notes while the contact is fresh. Keep an offline backup of your log. Official sources Software and network details change. title: Digital Voice for Beginners: DMR, D-STAR, C4FM and M17 | ZL3TOM
description: A plain-language beginner guide to amateur radio digital voice, comparing DMR, D-STAR, System Fusion C4FM and M17, plus talkgroups, reflectors and hotspots.
content: ZL3TOM beginner guide Digital Voice for Beginners: DMR, D-STAR, C4FM and M17 A plain-language beginner guide to amateur radio digital voice, comparing DMR, D-STAR, System Fusion C4FM and M17, plus talkgroups, reflectors and hotspots. ← All guides 01 What digital voice means A digital voice radio converts microphone audio into data, sends that data by radio, and turns it back into speech at the receiver. The radio signal is still RF; internet links may then connect repeaters, hotspots and rooms around the world. Digital voice can sound clean when the signal is adequate, but near the coverage limit it may break up or disappear rather than gradually becoming noisy like analogue FM. 02 DMR Digital Mobile Radio is widely used by amateur operators. You will meet DMR IDs, talkgroups, time slots, colour codes and codeplugs. BrandMeister and TGIF are examples of networks; their accounts and talkgroup behaviour are separate. DMR can be powerful but has the most terminology at the start. Get your DMR ID before programming a network-connected setup. 03 D-STAR D-STAR means Digital Smart Technology for Amateur Radio. It is an open protocol created for amateur radio and supports callsign-based routing, repeaters and linked reflectors. Your callsign registration and routing fields need to be correct. Learn the local repeater's instructions before changing link commands. 04 System Fusion and C4FM System Fusion is Yaesu's digital system using C4FM modulation. Many compatible repeaters can automatically handle analogue FM and digital C4FM. WIRES-X links participating stations through rooms and nodes. A radio displaying C4FM does not automatically mean every internet network or room is available; the repeater or hotspot configuration also matters. 05 M17 M17 is an open digital radio protocol developed by the amateur radio community. It uses open technology for digital voice and data, with reflectors used for linking. Equipment and local coverage may be less common than DMR, D-STAR or System Fusion, so check what is active in your area. 06 Talkgroups, reflectors, rooms and hotspots Talkgroup A DMR conversation group selected by number. Reflector A shared connection point used by systems such as D-STAR and M17. Room A named WIRES-X destination used by System Fusion stations. Hotspot A small personal radio-and-internet gateway. Its RF frequency, mode, operator ID and network settings must be configured correctly. 07 Start without the confusion Find which mode has local repeaters, groups or friends you want to contact. Choose one mode first and learn its basic terms. Use a known-good codeplug or local club guidance as a reference, but verify every frequency and callsign field. Listen before transmitting and leave a pause between overs. Keep radio firmware, programming software and codeplug backups organised. Useful distinction: EchoLink and AllStar are linked voice systems, but they are not over-the-air digital modulation formats such as DMR, D-STAR, C4FM or M17. title: QSO One Setup Guide: DMR, EchoLink and AllStar | ZL3TOM
description: A beginner QSO One setup guide for licensed amateur radio operators using EchoLink, AllStarLink, DMR, System Fusion and M17 on Windows or Android.
content: ZL3TOM beginner guide QSO One Setup Guide: DMR, EchoLink and AllStar A beginner QSO One setup guide for licensed amateur radio operators using EchoLink, AllStarLink, DMR, System Fusion and M17 on Windows or Android. ← All guides 01 What QSO One is QSO One is an amateur radio app that brings several linked voice systems into one interface. Its official site lists AllStarLink, EchoLink, IAX Direct, DMR through BrandMeister and TGIF, System Fusion and M17. It is an access tool, not a replacement for your amateur radio licence or the separate accounts required by each network. 02 Download it safely Start at the official QSO One website ↗ . Choose the official Windows or Android download offered for your device. On Windows, the official Microsoft Store listing is another safe source. Install updates only from the official site, store or app updater. At the time this guide was updated, the official site listed Windows 10/11 64-bit and Android 8 or later. It showed iOS, macOS and Linux as coming soon, so verify current availability before installing. 03 Prepare your accounts QSO One: create or sign in with your licensed callsign as directed by the app. EchoLink: install EchoLink and complete callsign validation first. DMR: obtain your own DMR ID from RadioID, then configure the network account you intend to use. AllStarLink: use your authorised node details. IAX Direct credentials must come from the node owner. Keep secrets private: never publish an IAX password, hotspot security password or network account password. Your public node number and callsign are fine to share. 04 First-run audio setup Allow microphone permission. Select the correct microphone and speaker or headset. Lower the microphone level if reports say your audio is distorted. Receive and listen before trying transmit. Use headphones if you hear echo or feedback. Only one application should control the microphone at a time. Close meeting or recording apps if audio behaves unpredictably. 05 Connect with EchoLink Sign in with your validated EchoLink callsign, search for the station or node, connect, and listen before transmitting. If a direct connection fails, follow the app's current proxy or fallback guidance. ZL3TOM EXAMPLE EchoLink node 304602 — ZL3TOM-L 06 Connect with AllStar or IAX Direct For AllStarLink, select the connection method you are authorised to use and enter the public node number where requested. IAX Direct is different: it needs the server, port, username and password supplied by that node's owner. ZL3TOM EXAMPLE AllStar node 40452 Do not guess credentials or use someone else's private node login. 07 Connect with DMR or other digital modes For DMR, enter your own DMR ID and follow the current QSO One instructions for BrandMeister or TGIF. Select the intended talkgroup, listen first, and identify with your callsign. System Fusion and M17 use different network concepts and credentials. Configure one system at a time so you can test it properly. 08 Troubleshooting checklist Confirm your callsign validation or DMR ID approval is complete. Check microphone permission and the selected audio devices. Verify the node number, talkgroup or destination. Re-enter private credentials carefully without sharing a screenshot containing them. Try receive-only first and then one short transmission. Check the official site for release notes, updated instructions and support. 09 Good linked-network operating Pause after keying, keep early transmissions short, and leave a gap between overs. Large talkgroups and linked nodes can cover many repeaters or users, so listen carefully and avoid long tests on busy destinations. FIRST CALL ZL3TOM listening through QSO One. title: APRS for Beginners: Radio, Apps and APRS.fi | ZL3TOM
description: Learn what APRS does, how stations exchange position and status information, ways to receive or transmit, and how to use APRS.fi responsibly.
content: ZL3TOM beginner guide APRS for Beginners: Radio, Apps and APRS.fi Learn what APRS does, how stations exchange position and status information, ways to receive or transmit, and how to use APRS.fi responsibly. ← All guides 01 APRS is more than a moving map APRS—the Automatic Packet Reporting System—exchanges local, real-time amateur-radio information. Position reports are familiar, but the system also supports station status, short messages, objects, weather data and queries using standard packet formats. 02 Start by receiving Open APRS.fi ↗ and search for a callsign or your local area. Watching stations first helps you understand symbols, paths, comments and how often different station types beacon. A receive-capable radio and packet decoder can also show local RF activity without transmitting. 03 Ways to use APRS APRS-capable radio: combines a radio, GPS and packet modem in one unit. Radio plus TNC: a separate terminal node controller or sound-card modem encodes and decodes packets. Phone app: software such as APRSdroid can display or gate information using supported radio or internet connections. Web map: APRS.fi is useful for viewing data that has reached the APRS-IS internet system. 04 Configure a station carefully Enter your own licensed callsign and choose an appropriate SSID for the station type. Select the frequency and packet settings specified by the current local band plan. Choose a symbol and short comment that accurately describe the station. Use a conservative beacon rate and a path suited to the local network. Test locally and check whether your packets are being heard. Long or aggressive paths and rapid beacons can congest the shared channel. Follow local digipeater guidance. 05 Protect privacy and safety Remember: APRS position reports may become publicly visible and remain available through internet services. Do not beacon a private home location, vulnerable person, or sensitive journey without informed permission. Keep attention on driving, mount equipment safely and never operate a phone by hand while moving. 06 If your station does not appear Confirm your callsign, SSID, symbol and packet format. Check the local frequency, audio level and squelch. Listen for packet activity and confirm an iGate is within range. Reduce path complexity while testing. Remember that APRS.fi only shows packets that reach APRS-IS; absence from the map does not always mean no RF station heard you. Official sources Software and network details change. title: AllStarLink for Beginners: Nodes and Good Operating | ZL3TOM
description: Understand AllStarLink nodes, linked radio contacts, connecting and disconnecting, operator etiquette, basic node setup and security.
content: ZL3TOM beginner guide AllStarLink for Beginners: Nodes and Good Operating Understand AllStarLink nodes, linked radio contacts, connecting and disconnecting, operator etiquette, basic node setup and security. ← All guides 01 What AllStarLink is AllStarLink connects amateur repeaters, remote-base stations and personal nodes using voice over IP. The network is based on Asterisk and the amateur-radio app_rpt system. A node normally has a unique number that operators use as its network address. 02 Nodes, links and the RF side Node A registered AllStar system identified by a node number. Link A network connection between two or more nodes. Radio interface Hardware that connects the node computer to a radio or repeater. Permanent connection A link configured to reconnect or remain connected; use only where the node owners permit it. 03 Make a linked contact Listen on the local node or repeater and identify any existing conversation. Use the connection method and control codes published by that node's owner. After connecting, pause so the network path can settle. Give your callsign, say which node you are using, and make a short call. Leave gaps between overs so another station can break in. Disconnect using the local node's documented command when you finish. DTMF commands vary. Never assume one node uses the same controls as another. 04 ZL3TOM node 40452 AllStar node 40452 and EchoLink node 304602 (ZL3TOM-L) are the two linked-radio nodes in my multimode system. Open the ZL3TOM AllStar Dashboard for node 40452 ↗ 05 If you want to build your own node Start with the current AllStarLink registration and installation information. A typical node needs a supported computer, a radio interface, suitable RF equipment, reliable power and internet, and correct audio and signalling configuration. Test locally at low power, confirm your audio levels and station identification, and follow the frequency coordination or band plan that applies in your area. 06 Keep the node secure Never publish IAX, SSH, web-admin or hotspot passwords. Keep the operating system and AllStar software updated. Restrict administration to trusted addresses or a VPN where practical. Back up the working configuration before making changes. Use only credentials and node numbers assigned or authorised for you. Official sources Software and network details change. title: How to Log Amateur Radio Contacts on QRZ | ZL3TOM
description: A step-by-step QRZ Logbook guide covering contact details, confirmation matching, UTC time, editing, ADIF imports and linked-network notes.
content: ZL3TOM beginner guide How to Log Amateur Radio Contacts on QRZ A step-by-step QRZ Logbook guide covering contact details, confirmation matching, UTC time, editing, ADIF imports and linked-network notes. ← All guides 01 Write down the contact first Record the other station's callsign, UTC date and time, band, mode, signal report and any useful notes. UTC avoids confusion between time zones and date changes. Check the callsign while the contact is still fresh. 02 Add a QSO in QRZ Logbook Sign in to QRZ and open your logbook. Select Enter Call or use the Add QSO option from a callsign page. Enter the contacted callsign. Complete the sender, receiver and QSL information requested. Check the UTC date, time, band and mode carefully. Save the record. QRZ's screens can change, so use its current help pages if a button has moved. 03 How QRZ confirmation matching works Each operator logs the QSO independently. QRZ matches key information including both callsigns, the UTC date and time, band and mode. Its current guide allows a time difference of up to 30 minutes, but entering the most accurate time gives the best chance of a clean match. 04 EchoLink, DMR, QSO One and linked contacts Log the actual contact details consistently and use the comments or notes field to record the network, talkgroup, room or node—for example EchoLink 304602, DMR TG 91, AllStar 40452 or QSO One. Agree on the details: QRZ confirmation depends on matching band and mode. For an internet-only contact without a normal RF band, check QRZ's current accepted fields and agree with the other operator on what both of you will record. 05 Correct mistakes carefully QRZ says a logged callsign cannot be edited; if it is wrong, delete the record and enter it again. Fields used by an already confirmed match can also be restricted. Review the official FAQ before changing a confirmed QSO. 06 Import with ADIF and keep a backup If another logger exports ADIF, use QRZ Logbook's Settings and Import function. Check your callsign, date range and time handling before importing a large file. Keep the original ADIF as a backup and inspect the import report for duplicates or rejected records. A good master log protects your contact history even if you later change websites or software. Official sources Software and network details change.
